<meta>continues from previous page: Mallinātha's commentary on the preceding verse, explaining "the news of a husband, brought by a friend, is to women little less than union with him."</meta>
<header>The Latter Cloud.</header>

of women whose hair is parted, that is, married women. "<term>Nārī</term>, <term>sīmantinī</term>, <term>vadhū</term> <gloss>all words for a woman or wife</gloss>," says Amara. **"Brought by a friend"**: brought, that is, received, through the mouth of a friend. The word "friend" is there to rule out any suspicion of deception. The news of the beloved is <term>kāntodanta</term> <gloss>tidings of the husband</gloss>. "<term>Vārtā</term>, <term>pravṛtti</term>, <term>vṛttānta</term> and <term>udanta</term> <gloss>all words for news</gloss>," says Amara. "A little less than union": only slightly less than contact with the beloved; the meaning is that it gives joy almost as union does.

Now he delivers the message:

O long-lived one, at my word, and to do a kindness to yourself,
say this to her: "Your companion, dwelling in the hermitages of Rāmagiri,
not dead, but parted from you, asks after your welfare, O tender one;
for creatures to whom misfortune comes so easily, this is the first thing to be said." ‖ 41 ‖

**"Her"**: O long-lived one. The suffix <term>matup</term> <gloss>a possessive suffix</gloss> is used here in the sense of praise; the meaning is, one whose life is to be praised for helping others. **"At my word"**: at my word, that is, my words of entreaty; and also "to do a kindness to yourself," your own self. The meaning is: to make yourself fulfilled by helping another. Although the self is the object of the act of helping, the genitive <term>ātmanaḥ</term> <gloss>"of yourself"</gloss> is not wrong when only a general relation is meant, just as in "he does a kindness to him." <note>Mallinātha defends Kālidāsa's grammar: the verb "to help" normally takes an accusative object, but a genitive is allowed when the speaker expresses a mere relation.</note> As Bhāravi says: "That is true wealth by which one does kindness to others." And likewise Śrīharṣa: "To do kindness to the good, to behold Lakṣmī, to travel through the sky." And so the dictum of Nātha, "somewhere a certain accusative, because it is not seen, so for all," is no dictum at all. <note>This sentence is partly garbled in the OCR; the sense appears to be that a contrary grammatical rule cited from an earlier commentator carries no authority.</note> Say thus to her, your beloved. Say what? He tells it: "O tender one, your companion," your husband, "dwelling in the hermitages of Rāmagiri," that is, staying in the hermitages of Citrakūṭa, <term>rāmagiryāśramasthaḥ</term>. **"Not dead"**: <term>avyāpannaḥ</term> means not dead. He gives the reason for his not having died: **"parted,"** having suffered separation and being in grief, he asks you about your welfare. Because the verb "to ask" belongs to the class beginning with "to milk," it takes two objects. <note>A rule of Pāṇini's grammar: verbs of the <term>duh</term> <gloss>"to milk"</gloss> group, including "ask," govern a double accusative, here "you" and "welfare."</note> For indeed, for creatures whose misfortunes arrive without any effort, "this alone," welfare alone, is **"the first thing to be said,"** that which must necessarily be asked first. The suffix <term>ṇyat</term> is used in the sense of necessity, by the rule "and the <term>kṛtya</term> suffixes." <note>Rāmagiri, the "Mountain of Rāma," is where the exiled yakṣa of the poem lives; Mallinātha identifies it with Citrakūṭa.</note>

With his limbs, so thin and fiercely burning, your limbs, so thin and burning;
with his tearful one, yours dissolved in tears; with his yearning, yours ceaselessly yearning;

1 "long-lived one" (another form). 2 "let him say." 3 "one." 4 "parted from you" (feminine); "appointed." 5 another reading of the last line: "for creatures to whom misfortune comes so easily, this alone; for beings whose senses are failing, this is the first comfort." <note>The second half of this variant is garbled in the OCR; the rendering is tentative.</note> 6 "O slender one"; "and thin." 7 "with flowing tears."

<summary>This page of the Meghadūta, with Mallinātha's Sanskrit commentary, gives verse 41 of the Latter Cloud, where the exiled yakṣa begins dictating his actual message to his wife, and opens the next verse on their shared suffering. The commentary explains vocabulary from the Amarakośa, justifies points of grammar with citations from Bhāravi and Śrīharṣa, and identifies Rāmagiri with Citrakūṭa.</summary>
<keywords>Kālidāsa, Meghadūta, Cloud Messenger, Uttaramegha, Mallinātha, commentary, Amarakośa, Bhāravi, Śrīharṣa, Rāmagiri, Citrakūṭa, yakṣa, separation, viraha, Sanskrit grammar, Pāṇini, variant readings</keywords>
